newsitem.title: SENEGAL: BOXING-SECOND "TYSON" LINES UP TO FIGHT HOLYFIELD.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-SECOND "TYSON" LINES UP TO FIGHT HOLYFIELD.

text.p: An African Tyson, Senegal's top traditional wrestler Mohamed Ndao "Tyson", is keen to take a tilt at World Boxing Association heavyweight champion Evander Holyfield's crown.
Mohamed Ndao, an unbeaten colossus aged 25, has just become Senegal's youngest ever champion at its national sport -- a hard-hitting mix of bare-knuckle boxing and more orthodox wrestling.
On Wednesday, when "Iron Mike", his more famous name-sake, was thrown out of boxing for biting Holyfield's ears, Africa's "Tyson" announced that he was considering following his hero into the ring.
"I'm a big fan of the noble art (of boxing) and I wish one day to pursue an international career," he told a news conference. "My wish is to fight against Holyfield."

Mohamed Ndao became the new star of Senegalese sport after defeating another titan, Tapha Gueye, alias The Tiger, in a weekend showdown that kept the West African nation on tenterhooks. It was his sixth successive championship win.

Traditional wrestling in Senegal has much in common with the Japan's national sport of Sumo wrestling, with fighters belonging to stables and training and living together. Fighters wear "magic" charms or talismen as part of their preparations.
"Tyson is my idol and contacts are currently underway for a possible meeting," Senegal's "Tyson" said of his hero.
He would not comment on the ear-biting, but acknowledged: "In sports some acts should be banned," he added.
Senegal's "Tyson", who enters the traditional dirt ring wrapped in the American Stars and Stripes flag, weighs in at 110 kg (242 lbs) and stands 1.92 m (6'3") tall.
Mohamed Ndao was the first Senegalese wrestler to travel to the United States as part of his training schedule.
"Whether you like it or not everyone knows that the world today is Americanised. I turn out with the American flag to make young people interested in wrestling," he said.
The day after his victory, thousands of happy, chanting young Senegalese paraded through the streets -- with American flags.
